title: How Earth was born (4.5 billion years ago)
sources: NASA Science: Earth and Moon formation pages (general)
USGS and Smithsonian explainers on Earth's age and early history (general)
Standard planetary-science textbook consensus (protoplanetary disk, accretion, differentiation)

verified.text: Chronological order of the story (tell it in this order): 1) the solar nebula, a cloud of gas and dust; 2) the young Sun and a spinning protoplanetary disk; 3) dust grains stick together into planetesimals; 4) collisions and accretion heat the young Earth until it is molten; 5) iron sinks to the core as the Earth differentiates; 6) the Theia impact, from which debris forms a ring and the Moon; 7) the Earth cools, a crust forms, and the first oceans form last.
The Sun and the planets formed from a giant cloud of gas and dust that began to collapse under its own gravity, about 4.5 billion years ago.
As the cloud spun and flattened, it formed a disk: most of the material gathered at the centre to form the young Sun, and the rest formed a disk of gas and dust around it.
Dust grains in the disk stuck together and grew into rocky bodies called planetesimals, some of them kilometres across.
Collisions between growing rocky bodies released energy as heat, and the young Earth grew larger by gathering more and more material.
The young Earth became so hot that much of it was molten, a sea of magma.
While the Earth was molten, heavy materials such as iron sank toward the centre and formed the core, and lighter materials rose toward the surface. This is called differentiation.
As the surface cooled, a solid crust formed. Gases released from the interior, including water vapour, collected into an early atmosphere.
As the surface cooled further, water vapour condensed into liquid water, and the first oceans formed.
The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, the age estimated from the oldest meteorites and rocks.
Mars-sized protoplanets and debris were common in the early solar system; the leading explanation for the Moon is a Mars-sized body, Theia, striking the young Earth.
The impact that formed the Moon happened early in Earth's history, while the Earth was still very hot and before the first oceans formed.

The Theia impact and the Moon forming from its debris must be told in their own line, separate from the iron sinking and the core: first the iron sinks, then, in a separate line, Theia strikes the Earth and debris forms the Moon.
The Sun and the Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago (लगभग साढ़े चार अरब साल पहले, 4.5 billion years).
Iron sinks to the core while the whole Earth is still molten, before any crust forms. The crust forms only after the Moon-forming impact, and the first oceans form last, as the surface cools.

theories.text: Scientists think a Mars-sized body called Theia struck the young Earth, and the debris from that impact formed the Moon. This is the leading explanation, not a certainty.

knownErrors.text: Earth formed in a single day or a few years
knownErrors.correction: Earth formed over tens of millions of years, and it was still growing and changing for a long time after that.
The Moon formed after Earth, most likely from debris after a large impact.
